feed.description: Software engineering conversations: reliability, architecture, delivery, and the tradeoffs nobody puts in the blog post.
feed.title: Practical Systems

bullets: A good on-call rotation is designed so that waking up is rare — the goal is to minimize pages rather than optimize response speed.
Alerting should be action-oriented — every alert must imply a specific response, otherwise it fails its purpose in the rotation.
Error budgets work when they change behavior — they only matter if they actually influence decisions and tradeoffs, not as a passive metric.
PagerDuty's incident response model assumes someone owns the page — the second-order effect of that ownership assumption is the part most people miss.
The framing of reliability decisions matters because it tells you which tradeoffs you're making — explicit framing beats defaulting into choices.
When teams adopt Sentry in that flow, the tradeoff becomes visible — tooling adoption surfaces the underlying reliability tradeoffs rather than hiding them.
If you ignore the tradeoff visibility, you end up rebuilding the system from scratch a year later — the cost of ignoring tradeoffs compounds.
A practical next step is to pick one of the covered ideas and run it for two weeks — the rest is iteration rather than wholesale redesign.
